What makes them so special? It’s because they turn on faster. Sooner. They get turned on way quicker than any other transistors. Yeah, I got a favorite transistor, the shiny fragile amazing mosfet. But the germanium, bipolar and somewhat easily startled and delicate, that loves getting turned on, is my most memorable transistor. Enjoy. She’s waiting for you, respectable and wonderful, the happiest of all semiconductors, the most delicate and perfect. Rock on. Where the Fat Fuzz Factory has a 3 position toggle, The FF7 has a nine position rotary switch and covers enormous sonic territory, from earthshaking low frequencies to “dog whistle” (figuratively) high frequencies. The Fuzz Factory 7 also has a passive tone control (with its own switch) to roll off high end if need be. Pedal Dimensions (LxWxH): 4.80" x 3.64" x 2.10" Instructions (PDF)

sources.excerpt: --> ZVEX Effects Fuzz Factory Demo Review | Loopy Demos Show or hide the side bar navigation Loopy Demos Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact All demos ZVEX Effects Fuzz Factory Mar 18, 2024 Read next What is the Best Velcro Fuzz Pedal? The ZVEX Effects Fuzz Factory is a certified classic, one of the wildest and most unpredictable fuzz pedals ever strapped to a board. ZVEX was one of the first boutique fuzz brands, hand painting circuits built around two new old stock 1960s germanium transistors instead of copying a familiar vintage design. I first went looking for one while chasing the guitar solo tone from Muse’s “Plug In Baby,” and found there’s a lot more on tap than a single fuzz voice. Five interactive knobs take you from a tight, normal fuzz to a velcro like gated chop to a sputtery, almost synth like oscillation. It rewards playing to it rather than through it: settings that look wrong will squeal and warble, and that unpredictability is the point. Controls Left to right across the panel: Volume sets output level, plain gain staging to match whatever comes next in the chain. Gate is the signature control. Clockwise, it squelches noise after your note decays, dialing out squeals, hiss and buzz until sustain quietly stops. Counterclockwise, it opens into the velcro like gated chop the Fuzz Factory is known for. Comp, which ZVEX’s manual spells out as Compress, adds attack rolled left, softens to the right, then suddenly pinches the tone into a squashed voice once near maxed. Its behavior also shifts with where Stab sits. Drive works like gain on a normal fuzz, pushing distortion and shifting feedback pitch and tonal thickness, though it stops mattering once Comp is dimed all the way up. Stab, short for Stability, is the wildcard. ZVEX’s manual says to leave it clockwise for a standard fuzz sound and warns that backing it off too far turns things soft and squishy. Open the Gate and pull back Stab together and the two fight for control as a note decays, which is how the Fuzz Factory gets into ripping velcro, shortwave radio warble and full blown self oscillation. In the demo above I’ve set up sweeps for Gate, Comp, Drive and Stab, plus the Noice Fuzz, Super Compressed and Garage Rock presets showing how they combine. How It Sounds Noice Fuzz keeps things comparatively tame: Gate high enough to keep noise in check, Stab low enough to lean soft and squishy rather than chaotic, so sustain decays smoothly instead of ripping apart. Super Compressed pulls the Gate wide open and pushes Comp near its ceiling, squashing the dynamics into a dense, pinched wall that swallows pick attack, exactly what the name promises. Garage Rock is the rawest of the three: Gate wide open, Comp off so full attack comes through, Drive maxed for the thickest distortion on offer, Stab in the middle for feedback color without tipping into full oscillation. The result is a punchy fuzz that behaves more like a loud rock pedal than an experiment. The Stab sweep demonstrates the manual’s own warning best: dialed down, soft and wobbly, dialed up, a stable, biting voice, while the Gate sweep runs the same arc from open, buzzing chaos to a tight, squelched cutoff. Fuzz Factory vs Woolly Mammoth ZVEX’s other fuzz with a demo on this site is the Woolly Mammoth , a useful contrast. It’s a four knob pedal (Output, EQ, Pinch, Wool) voiced for huge low end and a pinched, synth like bass fuzz that works just as well on guitar. The Fuzz Factory trades that low end weight for an extra knob’s worth of interaction, leaning hard into gated, oscillating chaos. For a thick, velcro textured fuzz that fattens up bass and guitar alike, pick the Woolly Mammoth. For a fuzz that squeals, gates and self oscillates into genuinely strange territory, that’s the Fuzz Factory’s reason for existing.
